notes: Section 288 challenge to inspector's dismissal of solicitors office appeal; Sullivan J rejected all six grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Bokhari v FSS: section 288 challenge to Forest Gate office appeal
key_facts: The claimant sought to retain office use at 26 Green Street, Forest Gate, in a predominantly residential terrace within Newham's Green Belt fringe area.
Newham refused permission for loss of a ground-floor flat, harm to street scene from a bay-window doorway, and amenity disturbance from office traffic.
The inspector dismissed the appeal, finding limited community benefit from the solicitors and immigration advice practice did not justify an exception to UDP policy H2.

The claimant challenged the inspector's decision on six grounds including inadequate site visit, narrow housing-stock assessment, area character, speculative amenity findings, and failure to consider conditions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application under section 288 of the 1990 Act to quash an inspector's decision dismissing a written-representations planning appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; Sullivan J held that none of the grounds disclosed any arguable error of law and ordered the claimant to pay the Secretary of State's costs summarily assessed at £3,197.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 288 challenge the court may quash an inspector's decision only for error of law or inadequate reasons, not because the inspector reached a different planning judgment on housing policy, area character or amenity where the decision letter adequately addressed the statutory development plan.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector conducted an inadequate site visit
Whether policy H2 community-benefit analysis was legally flawed
Whether the inspector misdescribed the residential character of northern Green Street
Whether amenity and precedent findings were speculative or unsupported
Whether the inspector should have considered planning conditions

confidence.notes: Each ground is addressed expressly and the application was dismissed with costs; no appeal outcome is recorded in the judgment text.

notes: Family injunction committal and costs appeals; Court of Appeal set aside unsafe findings and August 2003 costs order.

enrichment.short_title: Seiwa v Sankofa: unsafe committal findings and costs in family injunction case
key_facts: Mr Sankofa appealed orders made in bitter Lambeth County Court proceedings with Ms Seiwa concerning contact with their two children.
Judge Cox ordered Mr Sankofa to pay costs and adjourned committal proceedings; Judge Welchman later found two historic breaches of non-harassment injunctions but imposed no penalty.
The committal application was stale, diary evidence undermined the respondent's credibility, and the judge failed to compare diary entries with oral evidence.
Wall LJ set aside the August 2003 costs order for lack of means inquiry and explanation, and set aside the committal findings as unsafe.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from costs and committal orders in Family Law Act 1996 injunction proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; committal findings and associated one-fifth costs order set aside, and Judge Cox's August 2003 costs order quashed; Welchman's injunction remained until 1 October 2005.
enrichment.ratio: Where committal findings rest on stale allegations and diary evidence has damaged a witness's credibility, a trial judge must compare documentary and oral evidence before applying the criminal standard of proof; an unusual costs order against an unrepresented litigant requires explanation and a means inquiry.
legal_issues: Whether Judge Cox's costs order was justified without a means assessment
Whether committal findings were safe after long delay and unreliable diaries
Whether the burden and standard of proof in committal proceedings were correctly applied
Whether findings of contempt without penalty should stand on appeal

confidence.notes: Appellate reasoning on both limbs of the appeal is detailed and the final order is clearly stated.

notes: Landmark minerals JR on condition 10 interpretation and Whitley principle; 1971 permission held extant.

enrichment.short_title: Hart Aggregates v Hartlepool: ROMP application and 1971 quarry permission lapse
key_facts: Hart Aggregates sought new conditions under Schedule 13 paragraph 9 for a 1971 limestone quarry permission at Hart Quarry, Hartlepool.
The council refused to consider the ROMP application on the basis that condition 10 had not been complied with because no restoration scheme was agreed before extraction commenced.
Quarrying had continued for about 34 years and restoration was later governed by 1989 and 1996 permissions.

Sullivan J held condition 10 did not require a pre-commencement restoration scheme where restoration followed submitted plan levels, and that even on the council's view the Whitley principle did not invalidate long-implemented extraction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a minerals planning authority's refusal to determine a ROMP application under Schedule 13 of the Environment Act 1995.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; decision quashed and a declaration made that the 1971 permission had not lapsed; leave to appeal granted on interpretation and Whitley issues.
enrichment.ratio: Condition 10 of the 1971 permission is satisfied if worked-out areas are restored to submitted plan levels without a separate pre-commencement restoration scheme, and the Whitley condition-precedent principle applies only where a condition expressly prohibits development until approval is obtained, not to every restoration-related obligation.
legal_issues: Proper construction of condition 10 of the 1971 permission
Whether non-compliance with condition 10 caused the permission to lapse in 1976
Application of the Whitley principle to minerals permissions
Whether enforcement immunity and Hammerton reasoning affect implementation analysis
linked_authorities: FG Whitley & Sons Co Ltd v Secretary of State for Wales [1992] 3 PLR 72
Daniel Platt Ltd v Secretary of State for the Environment [1997] 1 PLR 73
Hammerton v London Underground Ltd [2002] EWHC 2307 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Long but coherent judgment with clear conclusions on interpretation, lapse and alternative Whitley analysis.

notes: Section 288 challenge to Suffolk Wildlife Trust barn conversion; inspector's decision quashed for inadequate reasons on expansion.

enrichment.short_title: Kernahan v FSS: quashing barn-to-office appeal for inadequate reasons
key_facts: Neighbours challenged an inspector's decision allowing conversion of barns at Foxburrow Farm for Suffolk Wildlife Trust headquarters and an education centre.
The inspector permitted the appeal subject to conditions limiting use and addressing traffic on an unmade lane off Saddlemakers Lane.
The claimants argued failure to assess baseline traffic, cumulative impact, and future expansion under local plan policy AP73(viii).
Judge Mole rejected error-of-law grounds on traffic but quashed the decision because reasons on future staff expansion were inadequate under South Bucks principles.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court challenge under section 288 of the 1990 Act to an inspector's decision allowing a section 78 planning appeal after an informal hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Application succeeded on reasons challenge alone; inspector's decision quashed; claimants awarded costs to be assessed administratively.
enrichment.ratio: An inspector may assess additional traffic without establishing a full baseline where that approach is open on the facts, but where future expansion could materially affect the decision the decision letter must explain adequately how that issue was resolved.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector failed to consider cumulative traffic impact
Whether policy AP73(viii) required express assessment of future expansion
Whether the inspector omitted a material planning consideration
Whether the decision letter gave adequate reasons on expansion and traffic
linked_authorities: South Bucks District Council v Porter [2004] 1 WLR 1953

confidence.notes: Final disposition rests on reasons inadequacy only; other grounds were rejected on merits.

notes: Costs-only appeal after nurse's fall trial; Court of Appeal restored normal Part 36 consequences.

enrichment.short_title: Alli v Luton NHS Trust: no-order-as-to-costs appeal after liability trial
key_facts: Mrs Alli, a nurse, succeeded at trial on liability after falling on an unlit hospital staircase but the judge made no order as to costs.
The judge considered her late trial evidence on corridor lighting a material change of case that had misled the defendants in settlement decisions.
The Court of Appeal held the critical issue had always been darkness at the bottom of the stairs and the lighting change did not affect liability.
The defendants had rejected Part 36 offers including an 80/20 split from 11 August 2003.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against a county court costs order made after a liability-only personal injury trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; defendants ordered to pay indemnity costs below with enhanced interest from 3 September 2004 following the claimant's Part 36 offer.
enrichment.ratio: A discretionary no-order-as-to-costs after success at trial requires a material change in the opponent's case affecting settlement conduct; mere refinement of factual evidence on ancillary issues does not justify departing from the normal CPR costs rule or Part 36 consequences.
legal_issues: Whether the claimant materially changed her case at trial
Whether the judge's costs discretion was outside Tanfern v McDonald limits
Entitlement to indemnity costs and enhanced interest after Part 36 offers
Relevance of late evidence on corridor lighting to costs

confidence.notes: Costs-only appeal with clear appellate order substituting normal Part 36 consequences.

notes: Bank guarantee retrial appeal; Holme v Brunskill discharge upheld on oral agreement and Hayward side letter.

enrichment.short_title: Lloyds TSB v Hayward: guarantor discharged after club refinancing variation
key_facts: Mr Hayward had given three guarantees totalling £650,000 to secure Bournemouth and Boscombe Athletic Football Club's borrowing from Lloyds TSB.
At a September 1994 refinancing meeting an oral agreement was made that calling Mr Gardiner's £250,000 guarantee for the June 1996 instalment would not trigger default against the club.
Evans-Lombe J on retrial found that oral agreement and that the Hayward side letter reinstated Holme v Brunskill by varying clause 8 of the guarantees.
The later Gardiner side letter varied the bank-club facility to Mr Hayward's potential detriment without his consent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal to the Court of Appeal after a retrial ordered on the scope of the September 1994 agreement and guarantor discharge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; bank's claims against Mr Hayward dismissed and he was held discharged from the guarantees under Holme v Brunskill.
enrichment.ratio: Where a creditor and principal debtor agree orally to alter default rights after a written facility is signed, and a side letter with the guarantor reinstates Holme v Brunskill by overriding a non-variation clause, a subsequent side letter between creditor and principal debtor that potentially worsens the guarantor's position discharges him.
legal_issues: Whether an oral agreement varied the September 1994 facility letter
Whether the Thomas note corroborated Mr Hayward's account
Construction of the Hayward side letter on renegotiation
Whether the Gardiner side letter triggered Holme v Brunskill discharge

confidence.notes: Complex fact-sensitive appeal but final disposition and legal analysis are explicit.

notes: Law Society intervention appeal; Court of Appeal upheld intervention and rejected extra-statutory remedy.

enrichment.short_title: Sritharan v Law Society: intervention on suspected client-account dishonesty
key_facts: The Law Society intervened in Mr Sritharan's practice under Schedule 1 on suspicion of dishonesty after large unallocated transfers from client to office account.
A client-account deficit exceeding £900,000 remained after injections and disputed unbilled costs; misleading mortgage certificates were also identified.
Hart J refused to direct withdrawal of intervention notices, restore the practising certificate, return files, or discharge a reduced freezing injunction.
The Court of Appeal held paragraphs 6(5) and 9(11) did not permit the court to fashion an alternative receiver-style remedy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited appeal to the Court of Appeal from Hart J's refusal of applications under paragraphs 6(4) and 9(8) of Schedule 1 to the Solicitors Act 1974.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; intervention, practising certificate suspension, file retention and freezing order upheld; leave to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where reason to suspect dishonesty in client-account handling is established, the court on a paragraph 6(4) application must usually allow intervention to continue; paragraphs 6(5) and 9(11) are ancillary and do not empower the court to substitute a bespoke extra-statutory supervision regime.
legal_issues: Whether reason to suspect dishonesty was established
Whether intervention should continue in the public interest
Scope of court powers under paragraphs 6(5) and 9(11)
Compatibility of intervention with Article 1 Protocol 1 ECHR
linked_authorities: Holder v Law Society [2003] EWCA Civ 39
Bultitude v Law Society [2004] EWCA Civ 1853

confidence.notes: Detailed appellate approval of Hart J on both jurisdiction and merits; no challenge to suspicion finding.

notes: JR on Crown Court post-trial refusal to permit tape analysis; judge held functus officio and granted declaration.

enrichment.short_title: West Yorkshire Police v Lincoln Crown Court: LPP and bugged custody tapes
key_facts: During a Lincoln Crown Court trial the judge ordered non-disclosure of tapes including legally privileged solicitor-client conversations recorded at Sleaford police station.
After the trial West Yorkshire Police, investigating for the IPCC, sought permission to analyse the tapes without listening to privileged content.
HHJ Heath refused by letter, but Sedley LJ held the judge was functus officio once the criminal process ended.
The police expert proposed technical analysis to determine whether surveillance was deliberate without violating privilege.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review by leave of Moses J of post-trial letters forbidding West Yorkshire Police from examining custody-area surveillance tapes.
enrichment.outcome: Application allowed; declaration that police may examine the tapes for IPCC investigation provided legal professional privilege is not violated.
enrichment.ratio: A Crown Court judge's trial order protecting privileged material does not survive to control post-trial investigative use by another force; legal professional privilege remains absolute but technical examination need not breach it where no listening to privileged content occurs.
legal_issues: Whether the trial judge retained power after conclusion of the trial
Whether analysis of tapes would erode legal professional privilege
Whether R v Derby Magistrates ex parte B principles barred examination
Whether IPCC investigation was pre-empted by the trial ruling
linked_authorities: R v Derby Magistrates' Court ex parte B [1996] AC 487
R v Lushington ex parte Otto [1894] 1 QB 420

confidence.notes: Core legal conclusion is clear though relief was by declaration rather than quashing order.

notes: UKIP market stall injunction refused; council obliged not to assist political publication under 1986 Act.

enrichment.short_title: Horsnell v Boston Borough Council: UKIP market stall licence refused
key_facts: Mr Horsnell, UKIP candidate for Boston and Skegness, sought to restrain Boston Borough Council from revoking his market stall licence during the 2005 general election campaign.
UKIP had used a subsidised stall in the royal charter market on Wednesdays and Saturdays after informal arrangements with the market supervisor.
The council's policy since 1998 refused stalls for political campaigning to preserve commercial character and political neutrality.
The judge held any licence for political publication was outside the council's powers under section 2(3) of the 1986 Act.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of an action for an injunction restraining revocation of a market pitch licence, treated by agreement as the trial of the claim.
enrichment.outcome: Injunction refused; claim dismissed because granting or continuing the licence would unlawfully assist publication of political material.
enrichment.ratio: A local authority may not grant financial or other assistance for political campaigning material it could not publish itself under section 2 of the Local Government Act 1986, and a subsidised market stall used solely for election publicity is outside its powers regardless of Hook fair-dealing considerations.
legal_issues: Whether the claimant had a term or indeterminate market licence
Whether Hook required fair procedures before revocation
Whether the council acted within powers under section 2(3)
Whether Article 10 was infringed by refusing a stall while allowing canvassing
linked_authorities: R v Barnsley Council ex parte Hook [1976] 1 WLR 1052

confidence.notes: Final refusal of relief and statutory ultra vires reasoning are clearly expressed.

notes: Green Belt mobile home section 288 challenge; claim dismissed on harm, special circumstances and written procedure fairness.

enrichment.short_title: West v FSS: Green Belt caravan appeal and written representations fairness

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Appeals) (Written Representations Procedure) (England) Regulations 2000

key_facts: Mrs West sought temporary permission until July 2007 to retain a mobile home and hard standing on Green Belt land at Rawreth, Essex, where she lived with her family.
An inspector dismissed her written-representations appeal, finding inappropriate Green Belt development and rejecting health, education and community special circumstances.
She challenged the assessment of actual harm, cumulative special circumstances, and alleged unfair failure to invite further evidence on health and education.
The court held the inspector properly assessed harm and special circumstances and that fairness did not require further inquiry under Dyason principles.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court challenge under section 288 of the 1990 Act to an inspector's dismissal of a Green Belt planning appeal conducted by written representations.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed on all grounds; no incompatibility found with Article 6 and no requirement for the inspector to seek further medical or educational evidence.
enrichment.ratio: In written-representations appeals parties must place all relevant material before the inspector; fairness requires further inquiry only in exceptional cases, and brief GP and school letters did not oblige the inspector to probe for additional very-special-circumstances evidence in Green Belt cases.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector failed to assess actual Green Belt harm
Whether special circumstances were wrongly considered seriatim rather than cumulatively
Whether Dyason imposed a duty of further inquiry in written appeals
Whether the written representations procedure was Article 6 compliant
linked_authorities: Dyason v Secretary of State for the Environment [1998] JPL 778
R (Singh) v First Secretary of State [2004] EWHC 2366 (Admin)
South Buckinghamshire DC v Porter (No.2) [2004] 1 WLR 1953

confidence.notes: Three grounds addressed comprehensively with clear dismissal on each.
